candidates.title: Ask HN: LLM-Resistant Publishing Strategies
candidates.raw_content: As has been discussed at length, LLM companies carried out the most egregious theft of labor [0] and intellectual property [1] in human history. I am one among the many (artists, musicians, writers, developers), who continue to be appaled at tech billionaires profiting from this [2]. As such, I have mostly ceased publishing original content online, while I wait for effective defenses to emerge. The two industry-standards are `robots.txt` and captchas. Neither works: the former is simply ignored, even by industry heavyweights [3]; the latter is trivial to bypass (using AI itself [4], remote solving services [5], or anti-detect browsers/impersonators [6] + residential proxies [7]). Emerging strategies include special fonts for creating OCR-resistant documents, tho current options don't seem to be effective [8]. Under the "dark forest" theory [9], paywalling or private distribution seem viable options, provided you can trust the recipients to not leak the content; of course, this is a death sentence for the libre ethos of the past 50 years, tho perhaps it was long overdue [10]. Please share your thoughts on any alternatives, real or speculative. [0] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49752056 - Microsoft exec called AI scraping 'the largest theft of labor in human history' (techcrunch.com) [1] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41275073 - Ex-Google CEO: AI startups can steal IP and hire lawyers to 'clean up the mess' (theverge.com) [2] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40297027 - StackOverflow is banning accounts that delete answers in protest against OpenAI (benui.ca) [3] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50401213 - Brave Sells Its Search Index to AI, and Your Website Is Probably in It (searchenginejournal.com) [4] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49930138 - Meta's Muse is fantastic for web scraping (sigh.dev) [5] https://captchathecat.com/ [6] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42547820 - Curl-Impersonate (github.com/lexiforest) [7] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48864252 - An update on residential proxies and the scraper situation (lwn.net) [8] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48873513 - Ghost Font: A font that humans can read but AI cannot (mixfont.com) [9] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47566442 - The Cognitive Dark Forest (ryelang.org) [10] https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50224074 - PHP Foundation 'under-funded' with one full-time staff member, director says (reuters.com) Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50411036 Points: 2 # Comments: 4

candidates.title: This sounds extreme and I wouldn’t have believed it even a year ago, but we’re starting to see plenty of examples of productivity gains that are an order of magnitude or two above output levels pre-AI. With the right harness, a deep understanding of your domain of what you want to build, likely a relatively new codebase (with some exceptions), a fluency of how to work with multiple agents at once, and a setup that makes it so you can test and deploy with limited friction, outputs on this level feel realistic in coding. What’s crazy is this gap doesn’t appear to be diminishing over time. You’d think that we’d see a convergence in the lines because of AI, but it turns out the more depth you had before -and willingness now to take a different approach- gives you crazy leverage. And that is only compounding as the models can take on larger work and harder problems. Right now this is most pronounced in software engineering for the obvious reasons. But there’s no reason we don’t start to see this in a number of other computer-use-sensitive domains like other scientific fields, AEC, finance, cyber, and more. Going to get quite wild.

candidates.title: The interesting thing about AI agents is that as a theoretical matter, their inference can kind of run anywhere. AI is one of the few areas of technology that isn’t *as* sensitive to latency back to the user. Long running agents are now going to be the norm, which means it’s ok to send off work to an AI factory somewhere and that work can essentially be largely done within that remote data center and a final result spit back to the user. The data can pass into these systems in an encrypted manner, be combed through by agents, and then disregarded right after. And because the economic value of the task is so high relative to the latency sensitivity (eg getting back $500 in value from an automated task, but it takes an extra second to return), you don’t have to have the inference to be particularly close to the user. Also, because inference is a temporary process with no sensitive data needing to be stored long term where the inference is happening, you can effectively treat AI factories as ephemeral systems, changing some of the data residency dynamics slightly. Combined, this means you have more flexibility in where you can begin to deploy AI data centers. This is both a huge economic opportunity for the states or countries (or space) that want to take advantage of this fact. And it’s a loss to the states or countries that decide to forgo the opportunity.
